book: 185 - Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades

chapters.relation: The editors introduce the volume by arguing that SNL, like philosophy, trains viewers to regard the world with a critical, questioning eye: four and a half decades of parody and satire wired generations of fans to think philosophically before they could articulate why. Land Shark, Spartan Cheerleaders, and Trump-era Update bits are cited as the shared generational memory the book will now analyze.

chapters.file: ch08 - Part I THE OPENING MONOLOGUE.md
ch09 - When the Subject is Not the Butt Schmitts Gay Beer.md
chapters.relation: Tallman asks why SNL may mock presidents (Chase's pratfalling Ford, Carvey's Bush) and Clintons but not unchosen groups, framing the question with the aesthetics debate among radical autonomism (Bell), radical moralism (traced to Plato and Tolstoy), and moderate moralism. Sketches from Samurai Futaba to Farley's Lunchlady Land show jokes can punch up, punch down, or elevate a low-status group. The Schmitts Gay beer sketch, she argues, ridicules not gay men but beer-ad conventions: swapping the usual female sex objects for men in speedos exposes the objectification and heteronormativity viewers had stopped noticing, so the butt is the advertising industry.

Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.

McGowan asks how SNL gets away with offensive material, from Larry David's concentration-camp monologue to the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' and 'Nude Beach.' He argues censorship fails because offense is historically relative and slippery-slope prone, and that on Mill's On Liberty the harm principle never licenses suppressing speech SNL viewers can freely avoid, a point he sharpens with Feinberg's Volenti maxim and the offense principle. He closes by defending offensive comedy as robust social critique: Mill's fallibilist case that free speech drives human progress, with Baldwin's Trump and Tina Fey's Charlottesville bit as comedians speaking truth to power.

Reynolds places comedy on a spectrum from philosophy to satire to smart-assery and argues SNL mostly sits at the silly end: Gumby, Mr. Robinson, Hermione's cleavage, and Hobbit Office are parody with an absurd twist but no constructive target, unlike genuine satire such as Mr. Bill. He develops the comparison through Aristophanes' Clouds, whose caricature of Socrates at the Thinkery helped send him to his death, and through the 'Playboy Philosophy' sketch with Belushi as Socrates. Socrates himself emerges as a satirist: the oracle of Delphi, his claim to know only that he knows nothing, and his elenchus that unmasks the supposedly wise are read as comedy in the service of seriousness, before the chapter concedes SNL's absurdism is philosophical mainly in mocking an absurd world.

chapters.file: ch13 - Part II SOME POLITICAL SKETCHES.md

chapters.relation: Irwin argues that SNL's caricatures (Fey's Palin, Baldwin's Trump, Aristophanes' Socrates in the Clouds) misrepresent their targets and that learning politics from comedy traps viewers in ideological bubbles, since satire flatters rather than informs. He introduces the Ideological Turing Test, adapted from Turing's test: state your opponent's view so accurately and sympathetically that a neutral observer cannot tell it is not yours, and grounds the duty to learn the other side from its own partisans in Mill's On Liberty. The 2016 'Bubble' sketch passes the test, he says, but SNL's liberal bias (gentle Sanders, untouchable Obama) rarely challenges its audience, and a conservative 'Live from Omaha' alternative would just rebuild the bubble on the other side.

chapters.file: ch15 - “We Always Have Something To Do”.md
chapters.relation: Engels uses Foucault's Archaeology of Knowledge, authorities of delimination, and power/knowledge to show that SNL now produces rather than merely reports political truth, as when the Fey-Palin sketch shifted media blame for the Couric interview from the McCain campaign onto Palin herself. The 2016 sketches (McKinnon's Clinton as the inevitable winner, David's Sanders as a fringe idealist, Baldwin's Trump as a self-sabotaging loser) are read as discursive framings that confirmed and shaped mainstream narratives. Like Foucault's doctors defining madness, comedy writers now set the boundaries of political truth, which spotlighted sexist double standards but proved dangerous when SNL's detached writers misread working-class voters; following Foucault's 'everything is dangerous,' she concludes we always have something to do.

chapters.file: ch16 - Where in the Hell is Chris Rock.md
chapters.relation: Wisnewski reads SNL's race comedy as applied philosophy of race: the Chase-Pryor 'Word Association' sketch shows Mr. Wilson's counter-slurs as an assertion of personhood against Mills's racial contract, Eddie Murphy's Mr. Robinson's Neighborhood and 'White Like Me' expose implicit bias and white privilege, and 'The Day Beyonce Turned Black' illustrates Du Bois's double consciousness. Appiah's racialism explains why Leslie Jones playing Trump strikes audiences as outrageous while white women play men routinely, and Appiah's biological anti-realism about race undercuts that reaction. 'Black Jeopardy' with Tom Hanks's MAGA-hatted Doug finds common ground across race that the 'Lives that Matter' ending sharply limits, Fanon's violence route is raised and set aside, and Crenshaw's intersectionality frames why cast diversity is more than skin-deep.

Irwin and addictions specialist Lombardo ask where comic inspiration comes from, using Socrates' discovery that poets do not know the meaning of their own work, Hume's account of creativity as recombining materials of experience, and Nietzsche's point that inspiration is really continuous production sifted by judgment, to explain why Belushi and Farley treated cocaine and alcohol as muses. They contrast Belushi's fatal 'I use drugs' hubris, which no one around him challenged, with Farley's genuine twelve-step recovery, three sober years, and relapses. Stuart Smalley's affirmations, which bullshit himself into feeling 'good enough,' spoof recovery culture's cliches while Farley's story shows what actual recovery demands, ending with the advice to look elsewhere for the muse.

chapters.file: ch18 - Part III SOME SKETCHES FEATURING YOUR FAVORITE RECURRING CHARACTERS.md
ch19 - All Human Experience is an Impression.md
chapters.relation: Ruetenik argues the best SNL impressions are not 'spot on': Carvey's Bush ('Not gonna do it. Wouldn't be prudent') and the Tom Brokaw pre-tapes sketch created new experiences rather than faithful copies, while Darrell Hammond's exact impressions made him a 'tribute band' without Carvey's artistry. Dewey's Art as Experience and James's selective attention, in which every perceiver is an impressionist ignoring the blooming buzzing confusion, ground the claim that all experience is creative re-presentation rather than tribute to reality. He then turns the point political: SNL casting Amy Poehler over a spot-on Black impressionist as Michael Jackson tells us something about the audience's own selective, and possibly racist, experience.

Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.

Holt reads Wayne's World as applied philosophy of play: Wayne and Garth's basement show is intrinsically motivated leisure in Huizinga's sense, free, rule-bound, absorbing, and outside ordinary life, and Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness' supplies the play ethic against the work ethic. Against Wittgenstein's claim that games cannot be defined, Suits's definition of games as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles is applied to 'A-sphincter-says-what?', the '...not!' game, and one-on-one hockey with Gretzky. The dark side of play closes the chapter: Wayne and Garth exclude and mock outsiders, and the leisure of their magic circle rests on unacknowledged labor like Wayne's mom's laundry.

chapters.file: ch22 - It’s Good to Be a Fan if ….md
chapters.relation: Barrett uses Bill Swerski's Super Fans to map a spectrum of fandom from casual to moderate to Super Fan, then applies Aristotle's doctrine of the mean to the virtues and vices of fandom: knowing trivia is a virtue (the Trekkies sketch), admiring athletic excellence is noble, but excess becomes licentious obsession, Shatner's 'Get a life!', heart attacks at Ditka's, and spending Thanksgiving with da Bears instead of family. Deficiency appears in bandwagon fans who lack commitment and loyalty, and the Red Sox fans' hospitalized heartbreak shows misplaced priorities in grief. Moderate fandom, loyal to people first and teams second, is the virtuous mean.

chapters.file: ch23 - Part IV AND NOW FOR OUR MUSICAL GUEST.md

chapters.relation: Gracyk argues that SNL's liveness lies in real-time broadcast rather than co-presence, rejecting the performance-studies claim that televised audiences see only simulations: a performance is whatever the performer frames for audience attention (Sparshott's isolating act of attention, Thom's for-an-audience condition, Davies's framing), and mediated viewing counts. On that basis Eminem's contested 'Mosh' and 'Bezerk' appearances either were not performances or were badly framed ones, since he failed to signal that his prerecorded vocal was meant as intentional doubling. Andy Kaufman's Mighty Mouse lip-synch on the 1975 premiere, by contrast, openly framed its own fakery as 'Foreign Man,' a Warholian act that made lip-synching itself the philosophical subject and so a great live performance about what performance is.

chapters.file: ch26 - We’re Here to Pump ‐clap‐ You Up! The Goal of SNL and “Weekend Update”.md
chapters.relation: Fried recasts Norm Macdonald's firing from Weekend Update as a philosophical dispute about the goal of comedy: NBC executive Don Ohlmeyer wanted wall-to-wall laughter and applause, guaranteed by recurring characters and celebrity walk-ons, while Macdonald hated applause as a cheap voluntary 'we agree' and aimed only at involuntary laughter he could not pander his way to. Eastman's play theory of laughter as an instinctive, uncontrollable response supports Norm, while Freud's relief theory, humor as release of pent-up tension, fits Ohlmeyer's comfort comedy. Fried concludes that if SNL is merely a comedy platform Norm was right, but as a shared cultural ritual that also comforts after tragedy, SNL may legitimately aim at more than involuntary laughter.

chapters.file: ch27 - A New Holiday Album A Lesson Is in the Lyrics.md
chapters.relation: Sudnick and Garrett stage the Dewey-Lippmann debate through Weekend Update's citizen journalists: Drunk Uncle and Girl at Party exemplify Lippmann's propagandized pseudo-environments and echo chambers, while Stefon parodies the expert gatekeeper his technocratic 'machinery of knowledge' would install. Dewey's The Public and its Problems answers that democracy needs public education, a free and publicly funded press, and wide participation, with Point/Counterpoint and Cathy Ann's plea to log off and meet face-to-face as comic images of deliberative citizenship. The chapter ends with Dewey's hope that artists, from Opera Man to Sandler's Chanukah Song, are the real purveyors of news in a democracy consummated by artful communication.

chapters.file: ch28 - That’s the News. Good Night and Have a Pleasant Tomorrow.md
chapters.relation: Erion reads Weekend Update as comic media theory built on Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death and McLuhan's 'medium is the message': television's entertainment bias shapes what its content can be, and SNL's fake newscast has demonstrated the 'Now...this' incoherence of TV news from the 1975 premiere's disaster teasers, Blaine Hotel slashings report, and Goggles-and-Pip feel-good story onward. Later sketches parodying Morning Joe, Dateline's Pervert Hunters, and CNN's animated reenactments keep the same critique alive for cable and social media. Because Postman himself proposed parody along the lines of SNL as television's only self-critique, the chapter closes asking whether comedy can expose TV from inside TV or is inevitably co-opted by it, leaving education as the last hope.

chapters.file: ch29 - Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View.md
chapters.relation: Southworth and Tallman use David Spade's 'falling star' joke about Eddie Murphy, and Murphy's twenty-year SNL boycott, to test three theories of familial obligation against the show's self-described 'family.' The role-based Just Because View, identified with Confucian filial piety, condemns Spade's disrespect toward an SNL elder but also forbids Murphy's divorce from the family; the contractarian Reciprocity View says Spade owes Dennis Miller but not Murphy, unless Murphy's saving the early show counts; and Jane English's No Special Obligations View, on which family should work like friendship, love rather than debt, clears Spade entirely. Sketches from the Vogelchecks' kissing family to Dysfunctional Family Feud supply the counterexamples.

chapters.file: ch30 - Part VI THE ABSURD STUFF THAT HAPPENS NEAR THE END.md

chapters.relation: Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.

Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.

chapters.file: ch33 - Where Do We Go from Here – Buh‐Bye!.md
chapters.relation: Southworth asks whether SNL's dumb characters, the Ladies Man, Celebrity Jeopardy's Burt Reynolds, Ferrell's Bush, can be too stupid for moral responsibility. Aristotle's capacity for decision grounds moral agency; the Merit View, sharpened by Williams's constitutive moral luck and the Control Principle, blames Ferrell's deliberately nasty Connery but not the hapless Reynolds; and Mill's consequentialist view of praise and blame as nudges for 'progressive beings' explains Stuart Smalley's affirmations and Gilly's scoldings. Strawson's reactive attitudes finally resolve the puzzle: pitiable Bush is no proper target of blame, which is why we love him, though making him so lovable may have helped the real Bush escape accountability.

holes.name: Ethical Criticism of Art (autonomism vs moralism)
holes.what: The aesthetics debate over whether moral categories apply to artworks: radical autonomism (art is judged only aesthetically), radical moralism (moral value supersedes aesthetic value), and moderate moralism (both count).
holes.why: Chapter 9 structures its whole analysis of punching up vs punching down in SNL sketches on this trio of views, and no taxonomy slug covers ethical criticism of art.

holes.name: The Offense Principle (Feinberg)
holes.what: Feinberg's liberal principle that the state may restrict offensive (not merely harmful) conduct only when the offended person cannot voluntarily avoid the offense, the Volenti maxim.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses the offense principle to explain why SNL's offensive sketches stay permissible, since viewers can simply change the channel.

holes.name: Aristophanes
holes.what: Athenian Old Comedy playwright (c. 449-386 BC) whose satirical plays, above all Clouds, ridiculed sophists, natural philosophers, and Socrates himself.
holes.why: Chapter 12 builds its satire-versus-smart-assery comparison on the Clouds and its caricature of Socrates, and chapter 14 reuses the same example of harmful caricature.

holes.name: The Principle of Charity
holes.what: The norm of interpreting an opponent's position in its strongest, most reasonable form before criticizing it.
holes.why: Chapter 14 argues caricature and satire fail the principle of charity and proposes charitable restatement as the ideal of political debate.

holes.name: Moral Grandstanding
holes.what: Warmke and Tosi's notion of using moral talk primarily to project one's own moral superiority, which fuels escalation, polarization, and devalued moral discourse.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies grandstanding to the Church Lady's Superior Dance and contrasts it with Sinead O'Connor's non-grandstanding protest.

holes.name: Philosophy of Play (Homo Ludens)
holes.what: The theory (Huizinga, Suits, Pieper) that play is a free, intrinsically motivated activity outside ordinary life with its own rules, and that playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire reading of Wayne's World rests on play theory, from the magic circle to Wayne and Garth's word games, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Liveness and the Ontology of Performance
holes.what: Performance theory (Sparshott, Thom, Davies, Auslander) asking what makes a performance live, what counts as viewing one, and how framing and technological mediation enter.
holes.why: Chapter 24 needs this apparatus to argue that SNL is live in real-time broadcast, that televised viewing counts, and that Kaufman's framed lip-synch is a genuine performance while Eminem's was a framing failure.

holes.name: Theories of Humor and Laughter (play and relief theories)
holes.what: Classic accounts of why we laugh, such as Eastman's play theory (laughter as instinctive animal play) and Freud's relief theory (laughter as release of psychic tension).
holes.why: Chapter 26 uses play theory and relief theory to adjudicate between Norm Macdonald's involuntary-laughter ideal and NBC's applause-driven comedy, and taxonomy lacks any theory-of-humor slug.

holes.name: Walter Lippmann
holes.what: American journalist and political theorist whose Public Opinion (1922) and The Phantom Public (1927) argued citizens navigate through distorted pseudo-environments and that democracy needs expert guidance.
holes.why: Chapter 27's Dewey-versus-Lippmann framing of Weekend Update's citizen journalists (Drunk Uncle, Girl at Party, Stefon) needs Lippmann as the expert-side pole of the debate.

holes.name: Neil Postman
holes.what: Media ecologist whose Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985) argues television's entertainment bias turns news and public discourse into incoherent show business.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is organized entirely around Postman's 'Now...this' critique of TV news as exemplified by Weekend Update, and he is absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Canadian media theorist famous for 'the medium is the message,' the thesis that the form of a communication technology shapes its content and social effects.
holes.why: Chapter 28 grounds Postman's argument in McLuhan's thesis (and chapter 27 invokes his retribalization for echo chambers), so media ecology needs him in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Filial Obligations (what grown children owe their parents)
holes.what: The debate over special duties among family members: unconditional role-based obligation, reciprocity for benefits received, or Jane English's view that only affection, not debt, grounds family duties.
holes.why: Chapter 29 tests all three views of familial obligation against the Spade-Murphy feud, and taxonomy covers Confucian filiality but not this Western family-ethics debate.

holes.name: P.F. Strawson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher whose 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) grounds moral responsibility in participant reactive attitudes rather than in desert or consequences.
holes.why: Chapter 33 culminates in Strawson's reactive-attitudes view to explain why SNL's lovably stupid characters escape blame, and he is missing from the taxonomy.
